kp.k: AI integration requires ongoing legal verification after rollout
kp.d: The feature describes integration as practical work beyond announcing partnerships or deploying platforms: refining prompts on live documents, checking outputs against playbooks and comparing model answers with senior-associate drafting. This presents human checking as part of implementation rather than treating deployment as sufficient.
qs: After the rollout, the work becomes practical as prompts are refined against live documents, outputs are checked against the playbook, and a model’s answer is compared to what a senior associate would have drafted.

kp.k: Early experimentation developed into a multidisciplinary innovation team
kp.d: The feature reports that A&O Shearman was Harvey’s first major UK law firm customer and began experimenting in September 2022, developing security and governance frameworks before broader rollout. Much of the subsequent work sits in the Markets Innovation Group (MIG), a 27-person team led by partner David Wakeling, with associates undertaking much of the practical implementation.
qs: The firm began experimenting with Harvey in September 2022, sandboxing the product and developing security and governance frameworks before rolling it out more broadly.

Much of that work now sits inside the Markets Innovation Group, known internally as MIG, a 27-person multidisciplinary team of lawyers, developers and innovation specialists building internal tools and client-facing AI products.
Inside MIG, much of the work of turning AI from theory into something lawyers actually use happens at associate level.

kp.k: Associate work expanded into governance and commercial software
kp.d: Susannah McMillan describes a progression from explaining generative AI to clients toward governance, guardrails and product work. She worked on ContractMatrix, a Word add-in built with Harvey and Microsoft, used internally and licensed to clients. Her role includes demonstrations, deployment discussions, tutorials and client relationships, extending beyond a traditional associate seat.
qs: Her work went from explaining what AI was to governance and guardrails.
She worked on A&O’s ContractMatrix, a SaaS Word add-in product, built in partnership with Harvey and Microsoft that is used internally and licensed to clients.
It includes demos, client conversations and what she describes as building relationships with clients, speaking to them about how to deploy AI and running product tutorials.

kp.k: Client demand shifted toward specific workflow problems
kp.d: McMillan reports that client conversations evolved from basic questions about generative AI toward sophisticated deployments targeting particular problems. This is her account of changing client demand, rather than a quantified market-wide finding.
qs: When I joined the team, I was joining calls to show clients Harvey and clients were saying what is generative AI? How does it work?
Clients are no longer thinking about chatbots or more kind of straightforward use cases. It’s deploying AI in a much more sophisticated way to help clients with very specific pain points.

kp.k: AI engagement became a deliberate career investment
kp.d: McMillan observes an internal shift from voluntary experimentation by enthusiasts toward recognition that AI capability can benefit lawyers’ careers. The feature presents this as an observed change in attitudes, not evidence of measured promotion or compensation effects.
qs: At the very start of AI being rolled out, it was a passion project for individuals who were open to using AI and excited about AI.
there’s been a recognition that it can actually really be helpful and useful for your career.

kp.k: Junior associates combine billable AI analysis with internal adoption
kp.d: Emma Jing, nearly one and a half years qualified, describes combining client-facing billable projects with internal adoption work. Her concrete example is using AI to compare negotiated agreements against a client’s playbook and template and produce deviation statistics. The account identifies an operating use case without reporting accuracy or productivity measurements.
qs: Now her days are a mix of client-facing, billable projects and internal work.

Today, for instance, I’m working on a client project, looking at a set of their negotiated agreements against their playbook and their template and using AI to work out how much it deviates and producing some stats on that.

kp.k: Adoption work balances risk awareness with process integration
kp.d: Jing describes internal adoption as encouraging use while making colleagues aware of risks. Her stated objective is to move beyond standalone chatbot interactions toward embedding AI in legal processes.
qs: It’s kind of a balancing act between making people aware of the risks, but also encouraging them to actually use it and seeing all the potential it has
Using it not just as like a chatbot, but thinking about how they can integrate it into processes.

kp.k: Hybrid qualification connects innovation with practice-specific automation opportunities
kp.d: Jade Low splits her time between funds and MIG through a hybrid qualification route. She reports that practice experience reveals manual tasks, particularly reviewing and comparing investor side letters, that she considers suitable for automation. This is an identified opportunity, not a reported measurement of realised savings.
qs: She is now on a hybrid qualification route, splitting her time between funds and MIG.

As I've been working in the funds team, I can really start to see the existing pain points felt by funds lawyers with really manual processes, such as reviewing and comparing investor side letters, that can really benefit from automation

kp.k: Prompting training evolves with models and client interest
kp.d: The feature reports that Low has run prompting training for colleagues and that the firm regularly changes prompting approaches following model updates. Low also observes growing client interest in AI and prompting within funds, which she characterises as historically resistant to automation.
qs: She has also hosted training sessions focused on prompting for colleagues as the firm regularly changes the way they prompt based on updates to the models.
Even in sort of retro areas such as funds, which have historically been resistant to automation, clients are starting to get really interested in AI and how to use it and how to prompt better.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The feature describes AI integration as ongoing, associate-led implementation work rather than something completed by purchasing and rolling out a platform.
pts.d: The feature's narrative locates much of this work in A&O Shearman's 27-person Markets Innovation Group (MIG), comprising lawyers, developers and innovation specialists. It describes refining prompts on live documents, verifying outputs against playbooks and comparing answers with senior-associate drafting. This is a human-in-the-loop account of implementation, not a claim of autonomous legal practice.

pts.k: McMillan describes a shift from introductory AI demonstrations to governance, product deployment and specialised client applications.
pts.d: Susannah McMillan reports that clients have moved beyond asking what generative AI is toward deploying it for specific problems. The feature describes her work on ContractMatrix, a SaaS Word add-in built with Harvey and Microsoft, used internally and licensed to clients. Her associate role includes demonstrations, deployment discussions, relationship-building and tutorials, extending beyond a traditional practice seat.

pts.k: McMillan reports that AI engagement has shifted from an enthusiasts' side activity to something lawyers perceive as career-enhancing.
pts.d: This is McMillan's observation of changing internal attitudes. The feature characterises lawyers as increasingly investing deliberately in AI. It does not claim a measured promotion, earnings or employment effect.

pts.k: Jing reports using AI in billable client work to analyse departures from contractual standards, alongside efforts to embed AI into workflows.
pts.d: Emma Jing describes reviewing negotiated agreements against a client's playbook and template with AI and producing deviation statistics. She also promotes internal adoption while communicating risks. Her stated aim is process integration beyond chatbot interaction; no time-saving or accuracy figure is supplied.

pts.k: Low identifies funds-document review as an automation opportunity and reports growing client interest even in a practice area she describes as historically resistant.
pts.d: Jade Low identifies reviewing and comparing investor side letters as manual work that could benefit from automation. Her hybrid funds/MIG role informs this observation. The feature also reports that she trains colleagues in prompting and that prompting practices change with model updates. The benefit is presented as a practical opportunity, not a quantified achieved efficiency gain.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims rest on three associates' first-person experience and named implementation examples, rather than quantitative evaluation.
pts.d: McMillan supplies experience of client conversations, product work and internal attitudes; Jing provides an example of a current client project; Low draws on funds practice and training work. The feature adds organisational context, including MIG's size and the Harvey and ContractMatrix deployments. It supplies no measured productivity gains, model-error rates, independent benchmarks or systematic adoption data. The embedded salary and revenue tables are not presented as evidence of AI effects.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The account traces changes from experimentation in September 2022 to current practice in the supplied 2026 feature; it offers no dated forecast.
pts.d: The feature says experimentation, sandboxing and security/governance development preceded wider rollout. McMillan describes an approximately three-year evolution in her MIG work, while Jing's project and Low's observations concern present activity. Implementation depends on continued verification, risk awareness, training and adapting prompts to model updates. Claims about broader process integration and side-letter automation are aims or opportunities, not predictions with completion dates.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The directly affected groups are A&O Shearman's junior lawyers, practice teams, multidisciplinary innovation staff and business clients.
pts.d: Associates undertake product development, client deployment support, AI-assisted billable analysis and internal training. Funds lawyers are identified as potential beneficiaries of automating manual comparison tasks. Clients receive AI products and support for specific workflow problems. Jing's non-technical background and Low's engineering-to-law and hybrid qualification paths illustrate differing routes into this work, without establishing a general recruitment trend. The source makes no concrete claim about junior displacement, staffing ratios, market-wide employment, fees or access to justice.
